7AYoXqCtME90flUOpBJM7i: Sean Penn made a film of Jon Krakauer's book about Christopher McCandless, a young American who finished university, gave his savings away to charity and went off on his own, on and on, until he got to Alaska. He didn't come back. A songwriter called Jerry Hannan had written this, and it ended up at the heart of the film: a man telling the world, without much anger, that he's going, and it'll manage without him. People say I've walked away from it all as well. About a mile and a half. I still row in for coffee every week, and the harbour shop lets me pay next time. Society, Eddie Vedder.
10ViidwjGLCfVtGPfdcszR: Alex Ebert and Jade Castrinos wrote this together when they were a couple in Los Angeles. The story goes she lost her shoes on a walk through Elysian Park, and he carried her home on his back. And that talk in the middle, about her falling out of his window, she's said that really happened: out of a second floor window, couldn't walk for a week, and he took her to the hospital. [dryly] Romance. Home, for me, is wherever Gerrit's crate is. I moved it one metre once, to paint the roof, and he wouldn't speak to me for days. Not that he speaks to me otherwise. Edward Sharpe and the Magnetic Zeros, Home.
6PnOqEt49VpxTv6gsq4U9S: Angus Stone wrote this on his own and first put it out in two thousand nine, on a solo record, under a made-up name. Hardly anybody noticed. A year later he recorded it a second time, with his sister Julia, and that version won the ARIA for single of the year back home in Australia and came first in triple j's Hottest Hundred. Same song, second go. I dropped my glasses over the side once, reading the label on a tin. The pair I bought to replace them are the exact same frames, and somehow they suit me better. Angus and Julia Stone, Big Jet Plane.
0fP0H7pj4phmIXO5wRJb2h: Marcus Mumford has never said much about this one. A very personal story, he called it, from a time in his life he wasn't proud of, and he left it there. Good. You don't owe anybody the details. There's a word in the chorus that got bleeped on most of the radio, and it was up for a Grammy anyway. Nothing gets bleeped on this boat, which is one of the few advantages of having no licence. I've got a thing I'm not proud of as well: a shopping trolley, a bet, a broken wrist, and for a month I told everybody at work I'd fallen off a ladder. Little Lion Man, Mumford and Sons.
50wmJUs9lJGDNRqJMUGH5F: Manu Chao made most of Clandestino on the move, years of travelling round Central and South America after Mano Negra broke up, with a guitar and a little four-track recorder that caught the street along with everything else. His friends called him the desaparecido, he said, because they never knew when he'd go or when he'd turn up. In Argentina and Guatemala plenty of people heard something heavier in it, the ones who vanished in their countries' wars, and I don't think he'd tell them they're wrong. When Opa breaks down and the station goes quiet for a few days, the fishermen ask over the VHF where Kees has got to. [deadpan] Under the engine, mostly. Desaparecido, Manu Chao.
0BF6mdNROWgYo3O3mNGrBc: Diplo first had this as a slow reggae song, and he sent it to Rihanna, and then to Nicki Minaj. Both said no. So it went to MØ, a singer from Denmark, and they sped the whole thing up, DJ Snake put in that bit after the chorus, and for a while it was the most played song Spotify had ever had. Diplo called the no's a blessing in disguise. I know the feeling. I didn't pick my shipmate either. Gerrit turned up in the third week and sat on the aerial, and the gulls I'd have chosen never came. Lean On, Major Lazer, with MØ and DJ Snake.
3m1JFLpKLYgMi1jf6Bu16P: Noel Gallagher had sung on one of their records before, and this was his second go. For the video they got Michel Gondry, and he took one dancer, Stephanie Landwehr, and multiplied her: mirrors, split screens, a whole chorus line of the same woman, after the old Busby Berkeley films and a television play Ray Davies made in the seventies. Pitchfork put it near the top of the best videos of the nineties. I've got one mirror on this boat, the size of a beer mat, and it has never shown me more than one bit of my face at a time. [dryly] Just as well. Let Forever Be, the Chemical Brothers with Noel Gallagher.
2cmRpmO04TLaKPzmAzySYZ: James Murphy put this first on This Is Happening, and it was the last song he finished. He called the title terrible, more or less, and the high bits cost him his voice while they were making the record. I know about that. I lost mine out here once, a whole week, with a cold I picked up in the harbour. I put records on and said nothing, and three bottles came by asking if I'd died. One just said: finally. [mock-serious] I've kept that one. What I wait for is the drum fill, just after the third minute, when everything he's been holding back comes in at once. Dance Yrself Clean, LCD Soundsystem.
4wWfO3quW5mDQZTiYeNnqS: The first version had a British group, Phi Life Cypher, doing the rap. Then the producer, Dan the Automator, wanted somebody else, and asked Del the Funky Homosapien, who was in the studio with him making another record. Del wrote his verses in about half an hour. He'd been working through a book on how to write a hit song, and then he forgot all about it, until people told him it was on the radio. The beat is the very first preset on an Omnichord. My transmitter came with a manual, the back half gone soft with damp, so I can only fix the things that go wrong at the front. Gorillaz, Clint Eastwood.
18AJRdgUoO9EYn11N7xzaT: Tove Lo says this is out of her own life: the stretch after a break-up when she was getting through it, in her words, not the healthiest way. The verses started as a poem. It took her about three years and five different choruses, and she put it out herself first, before any record company. Then an American duo, Hippie Sabotage, sped it up and pitched it up, and she first heard their version on a friend's surf video. [quietly] My first months on this boat I lived on beans out of the tin, the same spoon every time, and I called that a system. It wasn't one. Habits, Stay High, Tove Lo.
3aSjlsHzj8jaMt4iqGmkEw: Two and a half minutes, the perfect length for a boat. Sara Quin wrote it, one of the twins from Calgary, for So Jealous. Then the White Stripes put out their own version, and Tegan says it changed everything: they were on tour with the Killers, got a call about a strange video of Jack White playing their song, and went from selling hardly any records to selling thousands. [fondly] Somebody else telling your story better than you. The man in the harbour shop tells the one about me and the sandbank better than I do, and gets a free coffee out of it every time. Tegan and Sara, Walking With A Ghost.
0uVyZywUNOp6S0dU5r8TS8: Underneath this is a folk song by a French duo, Nili Hadida and Benjamin Cotto, from two thousand ten, and the words are about as bleak as a prayer gets: somebody who never wrote, and a world going downhill. Then a German producer, Robin Schulz, took it off the CD, put a beat under it and gave it away free on the internet. The record company was not pleased. A few months later it was number one across most of Europe. I've given this station away free for years. The only angry letters I get are from a ferry company, about something else entirely. Prayer in C, Lilly Wood and the Prick, the Robin Schulz mix.
2bEbTqj36jmuwMhvvCRC2y: Saffron, the singer, says this is about standing up to somebody who keeps putting you down, and she called it a battle cry for young women, back when radio wouldn't touch bands with a woman out front writing her own songs. The first time it came out it stopped at forty-three in Britain. They remixed it, faster, a guitar where the piano had been, and the second time it got to thirteen. Since then it's walked football teams out at Sunderland and sent people up a roller coaster in Ohio. I'd play it to Opa when he won't start, if I thought it would help. [dryly] He'd only want the pull cord, harder. Ready to Go, Republica.
6rxEjkoar48SssZePbtb2x: Oliver Sim wrote the first lines, about what a fling might be like, though he said he'd hardly had any relationships to go on. So he was guessing. He sent them to Romy Madley Croft, she wrote her verse back as an answer, and that's the song: two school friends from London taking turns, never quite at the same time. Jamie, the third of them, produced it. Talking to the fishermen on the VHF is a bit like that. One speaks, says over, and waits, and then the other one speaks. You can't both talk at once, and it makes everybody more careful with what they say. The xx, Crystalised.
1M5a4uGEeeptMgQB639oja: Win and Will Butler grew up in the suburbs of Houston, and Win said what set this album off was a letter from an old friend, with a photo of him and his daughter at the mall near where the brothers used to hang about. So the record goes back over all of it: the kids on bikes, a war that always felt like it was coming. It won Album of the Year at the Grammys, which surprised plenty of people. A listener once sent me a photo in a bottle: the ferry, from the harbour wall, and there's me on the car deck, small, in the hi-vis. [quietly] I keep it by the radio. Arcade Fire, The Suburbs.
25zLLjV2rWcOJwP7yUQIww: Brad Sucks is one man, Brad Turcotte, in Ottawa, recording songs at home and putting them online from about two thousand. This is off his first album, which he gave away for nothing, and then he put up all the separate tracks as well, so anybody could take his songs apart and remix them. Loads of people did. A song about getting jumpy for no good reason. I know it well. Every grey boat on the horizon is the inspectors for about ten minutes, until it turns into a fisherman, and by then I've let the kettle boil dry. Making Me Nervous, Brad Sucks.
5mhUPDWQH3s544WCsa0r9w: Brandon Flowers called this Johnny Cash meets the Pet Shop Boys. It came out of sessions with Stuart Price for another record, and he held it back because he thought it was too good for that one. Then everybody argued about the chorus, and the grammar of it. The line goes back to Hunter S. Thompson, sneering that America was raising a generation of dancers, and Flowers got fed up with people missing the point: it's meant to be danced to. On the ferry the bosun and I argued for years about the words of a song on the crew radio. We were both wrong, and neither of us ever gave in. Human, The Killers.
068LmtzI6xJJDPfPnMje0U: Kevin Parker wrote this in pieces, on tour. The verse walking to a hotel in Oklahoma, the chorus at a festival, the middle on a train to Toulouse with a loop going on his laptop. Then he took it all home to Fremantle and played and sang the lot himself. He says it's about trying to shut out the chaos of the world, and finding that keeping it out takes more out of you than letting it in. The first time the anchor dragged, I fought it for an hour: engine, chain, a lot of swearing. [sighs] Now I let her swing and settle. She knows where she wants to lie better than I do. Let It Happen, Tame Impala.
4IekHBYUwUNLILgA9R22OD: Damon Albarn made The Fall on his iPad, in thirty-two days, on the American leg of a Gorillaz tour. This one he recorded in Boston, on the fifth of October twenty ten, and to me it sounds like somebody a long way from home, watching people go round and round in a door. No proper studio, just what fitted in his bag. My whole station would fit in a fruit crate, apart from Opa, and Opa wouldn't go quietly. A few of the things I'm proudest of out here I recorded on a cassette, holding the microphone up to the speaker, and nobody's ever complained. Revolving Doors, Gorillaz.
15JwrZNa3W8WChqDuQevJy: Ásgeir grew up in a small village in the north of Iceland, and the words on his first album were written by his father, Einar Georg Einarsson, a retired teacher and a poet in his seventies. An old man's words in a young man's voice. I picked up a few things like that from old fishermen at the harbour, how to splice a rope, how to stand when the deck rolls, and I've never thanked one of them. King And Cross, Ásgeir.
7KCRCzZ8adIMdYODWNSOhe: Jake Shears came out to his mother as a teenager, on a family holiday, while they were getting ready to go and see Michael Crawford. Years later he was staying with his parents in Virginia when the chorus came to him in the shower, and he sang it into a little tape recorder. The song is the happy version of all that: take her out, show her the clubs, get her dancing, and she'll come round. I took Gerrit ashore once, in the dinghy, on a supply run. He stood on the bow the whole way like he owned it, and in the harbour he stole a sausage roll. [deadpan] He's not been invited since. Take Your Mama, Scissor Sisters.
0Ny4yM9JFFuCUZ497ouxKe: Björn and Benny wrote this on a trip to the Bahamas, and Björn says it started with a young fan he turned away because she was too young. So the words are a man saying no, more or less, while the music says something else entirely. Björn sang it himself, which hardly ever happened in that band, and they kept his vocal from the demo. Years later he said it would have been a bigger hit with one of the women singing. I often think this station would be better with somebody else talking. Gerrit agrees. He's never once offered. Does Your Mother Know, ABBA.
7safX55XidhznxK5eDdDm5: Mike Rutherford came up with the riff after seeing a jeans advert, the Levi's one with the Clash in it, and in the studio they called the song Blue Jeans. Phil Collins made up the words over the top, a dig at those blokes in the adverts who could walk about in jeans but couldn't dance or talk. They thought it was a joke, and put it out anyway. That stiff walk he does in the video he copied from kids at stage school, tap-dancing with their arms going one way and their legs another. I've had the one pair of jeans aboard for years. The sea has turned them a colour no advert would touch. Genesis, I Can't Dance.
76sAtRvVx4xIwHUJqyOpmb: This is the only time Jamiroquai went to number one in Britain. It was also one of the last things Stuart Zender played on, the bass player who'd been with them from the start, and he left while they were making the next album. Listen to that bass and you can hear what they were losing. In the video a cinema fills up with water, and Jay Kay said the extras weren't told it was coming, so the panic is real. [mock-serious] I can sympathise. The forward hatch on this boat leaks, and the first I knew about it was a wet sock and a tin of peaches going past my bunk. Deeper Underground, Jamiroquai.
5ELRkzdzz0HvGpMDlfZHkV: Harry Styles found the chords on a piano in Jamaica, and they recorded it there, in Port Antonio, the producer says in about three hours. Styles says it's a mother in a hard birth. She's told the child will be fine and she won't, and she has five minutes to tell it to go on and make something of itself. [quietly] That's a heavy thing to hand to a pop audience, and he doesn't flinch. I've worked out once what I'd say if Opa stopped for good. There's about five minutes in the batteries to say it on air. I won't tell you what it is. Sign of the Times, Harry Styles.
6QgjcU0zLnzq5OrUoSZ3OK: John Gourley was in the middle of mixing a different song, took a break, and started fooling about with the bass line from Please Mr. Postman, the Marvelettes' record. The verses, as he tells it, are a family man with a little daughter who still wants to kick up a fuss. It won them a Grammy. The fix on the transmitter that's still holding came to me while I was waiting for the kettle. Feel It Still, Portugal. The Man.
